resources.title: Global and Local Interpretability for Cardiac MRI Classification
resources.abstract: Deep learning methods for classifying medical images have demonstrated impressive accuracy in a wide range of tasks but often these models are hard to interpret, limiting their applicability in clinical practice. In this work we introduce a convolutional neural network model for identifying disease in temporal sequences of cardiac MR segmentations which is interpretable in terms of clinically familiar measurements. The model is based around a variational autoencoder, reducing the input into a low-dimensional latent space in which classification occurs. We then use the recently developed `concept activation vector' technique to associate concepts which are diagnostically meaningful (eg. clinical biomarkers such as `low left-ventricular ejection fraction') to certain vectors in the latent space. These concepts are then qualitatively inspected by observing the change in the image domain resulting from interpolations in the latent space in the direction of these vectors. As a result, when the model classifies images it is also capable of providing naturally interpretable concepts relevant to that classification and demonstrating the meaning of those concepts in the image domain. Our approach is demonstrated on the UK Biobank cardiac MRI dataset where we detect the presence of coronary artery disease.

resources.title: Concept attribution: Explaining CNN decisions to physicians
resources.abstract: Deep learning explainability is often reached by gradient-based approaches that attribute the network output to perturbations of the input pixels. However, the relevance of input pixels may be difficult to relate to relevant image features in some applications, e.g. diagnostic measures in medical imaging. The framework described in this paper shifts the attribution focus from pixel values to user-defined concepts. By checking if certain diagnostic measures are present in the learned representations, experts can explain and entrust the network output. Being post-hoc, our method does not alter the network training and can be easily plugged into the latest state-of-the-art convolutional networks. This paper presents the main components of the framework for attribution to concepts, in addition to the introduction of a spatial pooling operation on top of the feature maps to obtain a solid interpretability analysis. Furthermore, regularized regression is analyzed as a solution to the regression overfitting in high-dimensionality latent spaces. The versatility of the proposed approach is shown by experiments on two medical applications, namely histopathology and retinopathy, and on one non-medical task, the task of handwritten digit classification. The obtained explanations are in line with clinicians' guidelines and complementary to widely used visualization tools such as saliency maps.

sample_claims.text: The chest X-ray classifier's 'pneumonia' predictions are significantly sensitive to clinically recognised findings and not significantly sensitive to scanner type or patient positioning, at the layers tested.

The content-tagging classifier's TCAV scores for the ethnicity and gender concept sets are recorded for every output class at the tested layers, and the classes with significant sensitivity are listed for review.
The traffic-sign classifier's sensitivity to graffiti, snow cover and glare concepts is documented with significance-tested TCAV scores for each sign class the approval authority has requested.
The object recogniser's class predictions depend mainly on concepts that domain experts regard as meaningful for that class, such as shape and texture, rather than on background concepts.

techniques.name: Fairness GAN
techniques.description: Fairness GAN is a pre-processing method that generates a synthetic training dataset in which decisions no longer track a protected attribute such as gender or skin tone. A generative adversarial network (GAN) is a pair of networks trained against each other, one producing fake examples and one trying to tell them from real ones. Here the generator is conditioned on the protected attribute and produces both an example and its decision label, such as hired or rejected (images in the original work, table rows in Xu et al.'s separate FairGAN). An extra network tries to predict the protected attribute from the generated output, and the generator is rewarded for defeating it, so favourable decisions become more similar across groups. The user can aim for demographic parity, meaning equal rates of favourable decisions, or for equality of opportunity, which applies the constraint only to favourable decisions.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment technology team holds interview-video stills labelled with past shortlisting decisions that favoured one gender. It trains a Fairness GAN to generate a synthetic image set whose shortlisting labels are similar for women and men, trains the screening model on that set, and compares shortlisting rates by gender on held-out real images before deployment.

A lender's data science team has ten years of loan decisions in which women were approved less often than men on similar incomes. It trains a tabular FairGAN-style generator to produce a synthetic dataset, confirms that the gap in approval rates in the synthetic data is close to zero, and trains its scoring model on that data, testing accuracy and approval rates on real held-out applications.

limitations.description: GAN training is unstable and the fairness loss adds a further pull on the generator. The original authors used spectral normalisation, softened outcome values and added noise to keep training stable, and results still varied across datasets. Expect tuning effort and repeated runs.

Fairness and accuracy trade off, and the gain is uneven. In the original experiments a classifier trained on debiased CelebA data went from about 20 to about 29 per cent error. Demographic parity improved on three of four datasets but not on Quick, Draw!, and the demographic-parity version made equality of opportunity worse on the soccer data.

It needs a lot of data. The authors had only 1,501 labelled soccer images, so they borrowed more than 200,000 unlabelled CelebA faces to help the generator, which is possible only when a large related set exists.

The original method covers a narrow setting: image inputs, one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome, with demographic parity or equality of opportunity but not equalised odds. Continuous protected attributes and non-image data are left as future work, and tabular versions such as FairGAN are separate methods with their own evidence.

Fairness is judged by training a classifier on the synthetic data and testing it on real data, and image quality is judged mainly by inspecting average faces. The authors report that debiasing visibly changes images in stereotyped ways, such as male faces taking on features coded as feminine, so the synthetic data need checking for distortions that the classifier test would miss.

resources.title: Fairness GAN
resources.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Fairness GAN, an approach for generating a dataset that is plausibly similar to a given multimedia dataset, but is more fair with respect to protected attributes in allocative decision making. We propose a novel auxiliary classifier GAN that strives for demographic parity or equality of opportunity and show empirical results on several datasets, including the CelebFaces Attributes (CelebA) dataset, the Quick, Draw!\ dataset, and a dataset of soccer player images and the offenses they were called for. The proposed formulation is well-suited to absorbing unlabeled data; we leverage this to augment the soccer dataset with the much larger CelebA dataset. The methodology tends to improve demographic parity and equality of opportunity while generating plausible images.

resources.title: FairGAN: Fairness-aware Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Fairness-aware learning is increasingly important in data mining. Discrimination prevention aims to prevent discrimination in the training data before it is used to conduct predictive analysis. In this paper, we focus on fair data generation that ensures the generated data is discrimination free. Inspired by generative adversarial networks (GAN), we present fairness-aware generative adversarial networks, called FairGAN, which are able to learn a generator producing fair data and also preserving good data utility. Compared with the naive fair data generation models, FairGAN further ensures the classifiers which are trained on generated data can achieve fair classification on real data. Experiments on a real dataset show the effectiveness of FairGAN.

resources.title: Bt-GAN: Generating Fair Synthetic Healthdata via Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Synthetic data generation offers a promising solution to enhance the usefulness of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) by generating realistic de-identified data. However, the existing literature primarily focuses on the quality of synthetic health data, neglecting the crucial aspect of fairness in downstream predictions. Consequently, models trained on synthetic EHR have faced criticism for producing biased outcomes in target tasks. These biases can arise from either spurious correlations between features or the failure of models to accurately represent sub-groups. To address these concerns, we present Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks (Bt-GAN), a GAN-based synthetic data generator specifically designed for the healthcare domain. In order to tackle spurious correlations (i), we propose an information-constrained Data Generation Process (DGP) that enables the generator to learn a fair deterministic transformation based on a well-defined notion of algorithmic fairness. To overcome the challenge of capturing exact sub-group representations (ii), we incentivize the generator to preserve sub-group densities through score-based weighted sampling. This approach compels the generator to learn from underrepresented regions of the data manifold. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) database. Our results demonstrate that Bt-GAN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while significantly improving fairness and minimizing bias amplification. Furthermore, we perform an in-depth explainability analysis to provide additional evidence supporting the validity of our study. In conclusion, our research introduces a novel and professional approach to addressing the limitations of synthetic data generation in the healthcare domain. By incorporating fairness considerations and leveraging advanced techniques such as GANs, we pave the way for more reliable and unbiased predictions in healthcare applications.

resources.title: FairFinGAN: Fairness-Aware Synthetic Financial Data Generation
resources.abstract: Financial datasets often suffer from bias that can lead to unfair decision-making in automated systems. In this work, we propose FairFinGAN, a WGAN-based framework designed to generate synthetic financial data while mitigating bias with respect to the protected attribute. Our approach incorporates fairness constraints directly into the training process through a classifier, ensuring that the synthetic data is both fair and preserves utility for downstream predictive tasks. We evaluate our proposed model on five real-world financial datasets and compare it with existing GAN-based data generation methods. Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior fairness metrics without significant loss in data utility, demonstrating its potential as a tool for bias-aware data generation in financial applications.

sample_claims.text: In the synthetic training set generated for the screening model, the rate of favourable shortlisting decisions for women and men differs by less than the tolerance set in the project's fairness requirement.
A credit scoring model trained on the synthetic loan data shows a smaller gap in approval rates between women and men, on held-out real applications, than a model trained on the original data.
The synthetic data remain close enough to the original for the model's purpose: the accuracy cost of training on them, compared with the original data, was measured and judged acceptable.

techniques.name: Meta Fair Classifier
techniques.description: The meta fair classifier is a general-purpose training algorithm for fair classification. The user chooses a fairness metric, such as the statistical rate (each group's share of favourable outcomes) or the false discovery rate (the share of positive predictions that are wrong), and a target between 0 and 1 for how close to equal the groups' values must be. From labelled training examples that include the protected attribute, the algorithm fits a model of the data, solves a series of constrained optimisation problems, and returns the most accurate classifier that meets the target. It trains a new classifier rather than adjusting an existing one. The original paper proves the result comes close to the best classifier that meets the target, up to the error in the fitted model of the data.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment platform trains a shortlisting classifier with a statistical-rate target of 0.8, so that the selection rate for any gender group is at least 80% of the highest group's rate, and measures how much accuracy it gives up to reach that target.

A probation service building a recidivism risk classifier constrains false discovery rate parity, so that among people flagged as high risk, the share who do not go on to reoffend is similar across racial groups.

A hospital building a classifier for heart conditions constrains false discovery rate parity, so that false alarms, which send people for unnecessary medical attention, do not fall more heavily on women than on men.

limitations.description: It is a self-contained learner, not a wrapper. It cannot adjust a model you already run, and the paper lists extension to other classifier types as future work. It also needs the protected attribute for every training example, and teams must be willing to replace their model with the one it produces.

The AIF360 implementation supports only statistical rate and false discovery rate, and raises an error for any other metric. The paper's framework covers more, but other criteria, such as equalised odds, mean extra implementation work or choosing a different technique.

The guarantee depends on how well the fitted model of the data matches the real distribution, and the paper's bound carries error terms for any mismatch. In its experiments, a simple fitted model gave lower accuracy than competing methods at the same fairness level.
Results can vary from run to run. In a credit-scoring comparison, repeated runs sometimes missed the fairness target, which made averaging the results unusable.

The method solves a separate constrained optimisation problem for each value on a grid set by the tolerance, and the number multiplies for each additional fairness metric constrained at once. Combining several criteria quickly makes training slow.

resources.title: Classification with Fairness Constraints
resources.abstract: Developing classification algorithms that are fair with respect to sensitive attributes of the data is an important problem due to the increased deployment of classification algorithms in societal contexts. Several recent works have focused on studying classification with respect to specific fairness metrics, modeled the corresponding fair classification problem as constrained optimization problems, and developed tailored algorithms to solve them. Despite this, there still remain important metrics for which there are no fair classifiers with theoretical guarantees; primarily because the resulting optimization problem is non-convex. The main contribution of this paper is a meta-algorithm for classification that can take as input a general class of fairness constraints with respect to multiple non-disjoint and multi-valued sensitive attributes, and which comes with provable guarantees. In particular, our algorithm can handle non-convex "linear fractional" constraints (which includes fairness constraints such as predictive parity) for which no prior algorithm was known. Key to our results is an algorithm for a family of classification problems with convex constraints along with a reduction from classification problems with linear fractional constraints to this family. Empirically, we observe that our algorithm is fast, can achieve near-perfect fairness with respect to various fairness metrics, and the loss in accuracy due to the imposed fairness constraints is often small.

resources.title: Algorithmic decision making methods for fair credit scoring
resources.abstract: The effectiveness of machine learning in evaluating the creditworthiness of loan applicants has been demonstrated for a long time. However, there is concern that the use of automated decision-making processes may result in unequal treatment of groups or individuals, potentially leading to discriminatory outcomes. This paper seeks to address this issue by evaluating the effectiveness of 12 leading bias mitigation methods across 5 different fairness metrics, as well as assessing their accuracy and potential profitability for financial institutions. Through our analysis, we have identified the challenges associated with achieving fairness while maintaining accuracy and profitabiliy, and have highlighted both the most successful and least successful mitigation methods. Ultimately, our research serves to bridge the gap between experimental machine learning and its practical applications in the finance industry.

resources.title: Fairness in credit scoring: Assessment, implementation and profit implications
resources.abstract: The rise of algorithmic decision-making has spawned much research on fair machine learning (ML). Financial institutions use ML for building risk scorecards that support a range of credit-related decisions. Yet, the literature on fair ML in credit scoring is scarce. The paper makes three contributions. First, we revisit statistical fairness criteria and examine their adequacy for credit scoring. Second, we catalog algorithmic options for incorporating fairness goals in the ML model development pipeline. Last, we empirically compare different fairness processors in a profit-oriented credit scoring context using real-world data. The empirical results substantiate the evaluation of fairness measures, identify suitable options to implement fair credit scoring, and clarify the profit-fairness trade-off in lending decisions. We find that multiple fairness criteria can be approximately satisfied at once and recommend separation as a proper criterion for measuring the fairness of a scorecard. We also find fair in-processors to deliver a good balance between profit and fairness and show that algorithmic discrimination can be reduced to a reasonable level at a relatively low cost. The codes corresponding to the paper are available on GitHub.

sample_claims.text: On held-out data, the shortlisting classifier's selection rate for each gender group is at least 80% of the highest group's rate.
Among people the recidivism model flags as high risk, the share who do not reoffend differs between racial groups by no more than the agreed tolerance.
The share of false alarms among the heart-condition classifier's positive predictions is similar for women and men, with the accuracy cost against an unconstrained classifier reported.

techniques.name: Exponentiated Gradient Reduction
techniques.description: Exponentiated gradient reduction trains a classifier that satisfies a chosen fairness criterion, such as demographic parity (equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups) or equalised odds (equal error rates across groups), while keeping error as low as it can. It reduces the problem to a series of ordinary training runs on the same data, each with different example weights. Between runs, a multiplicative update, the exponentiated gradient step, increases the weight on fairness constraints that are currently violated, and a standard classifier is retrained on the reweighted data. The output is a randomised classifier, a weighted mix of the classifiers trained along the way, with one drawn at random for each prediction. The original paper proves that its error and its fairness violation come close to the best achievable, up to a tolerance the user sets and the statistical error from a finite training set.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment team trains a shortlisting model under a demographic parity constraint so that selection rates are equal across gender groups, and sweeps the method's tolerance setting to see how much accuracy each step towards equality costs.

A justice agency building a recidivism risk model trains a logistic regression under a demographic parity constraint on race, then compares accuracy and fairness metrics against the unconstrained model on the same data before deciding whether to deploy it.

A lender trying equalised odds, true-positive-rate difference and demographic parity as constraints on its credit-scoring model picks the one that gives the best balance of accuracy and profit on its own data, since the best choice differs between datasets.

limitations.description: The guarantees assume the base learner can solve each weighted training problem close to exactly. Real learners only approximate this, so the stated bounds on error and fairness violation are approximate in practice. The learner must also accept per-example weights, which rules out some model types.

The result is a randomised mix of classifiers, so the same input can receive different predictions on repeat requests. This is hard to defend where decisions must be repeatable, as in appeals or audits.

Needs the protected attribute for every training example, although not at prediction time. It enforces one fairness criterion at a time, and the original paper leaves trading off several criteria as an open problem.

Each round retrains the base model, and the number of rounds needed grows with the square of the inverse of the tolerance, so halving the tolerance roughly quadruples training cost. Large datasets or slow models make tight tolerances expensive.

Constraint violation is controlled only up to sampling error, which is larger for small groups. In one credit-scoring comparison the best-performing constraint differed between datasets, so the right criterion has to be found by experiment on the data in hand.

resources.title: A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification
resources.abstract: We present a systematic approach for achieving fairness in a binary classification setting. While we focus on two well-known quantitative definitions of fairness, our approach encompasses many other previously studied definitions as special cases. The key idea is to reduce fair classification to a sequence of cost-sensitive classification problems, whose solutions yield a randomized classifier with the lowest (empirical) error subject to the desired constraints. We introduce two reductions that work for any representation of the cost-sensitive classifier and compare favorably to prior baselines on a variety of data sets, while overcoming several of their disadvantages.

resources.title: Algorithmic decision making methods for fair credit scoring
resources.abstract: The effectiveness of machine learning in evaluating the creditworthiness of loan applicants has been demonstrated for a long time. However, there is concern that the use of automated decision-making processes may result in unequal treatment of groups or individuals, potentially leading to discriminatory outcomes. This paper seeks to address this issue by evaluating the effectiveness of 12 leading bias mitigation methods across 5 different fairness metrics, as well as assessing their accuracy and potential profitability for financial institutions. Through our analysis, we have identified the challenges associated with achieving fairness while maintaining accuracy and profitabiliy, and have highlighted both the most successful and least successful mitigation methods. Ultimately, our research serves to bridge the gap between experimental machine learning and its practical applications in the finance industry.

resources.title: A fairness-focused approach to recidivism prediction: implications for accuracy, trust, and equity
resources.abstract: Fairness in AI has emerged as a critical priority, particularly in high-stakes domains like criminal justice, where algorithmic decisions profoundly affect individuals and demographic groups. This study addresses persistent challenges of bias in recidivism prediction by evaluating the integrated application of fairness-enhancing techniques across the AI pipeline. Specifically, we analyze the integrated use of Reweighing, Adversarial Learning, Disparate Impact Remover, Exponentiated Gradient Reduction, Reject Option Classification, and Equalized Odds optimization. These methods are assessed using key fairness metrics, Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), Disparate Impact (DI), Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD), and Predictive Equality Difference (PED), on two real-world recidivism datasets: COMPAS, a well-known publicly available dataset, and RisCanvi, a curated English dataset derived from a publicly available Spanish dataset. Our findings reveal trade-offs between fairness improvements and predictive accuracy, with fairness performance varying across integrated mitigation strategies. While individual techniques often fall short of effectively reducing bias, their integration across pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing stages demonstrates a more comprehensive and robust capacity to address fairness concerns. In some instances, fairness mitigation strategies exacerbate disparities instead of reducing them, highlighting the complexity of achieving equitable AI outcomes. Some methods struggle with specific datasets, leading to worsened SPD, DI, EOD, or PED values, potentially reinforcing biases rather than eliminating them. Using multi-objective and bi-objective optimization frameworks, we identify optimal configurations that balance fairness and accuracy, contributing to a deeper understanding of fairness–accuracy trade-offs in AI systems. This study makes a novel contribution by systematically evaluating multi-phase fairness integration in recidivism prediction, bridging critical gaps in the literature. However, our results also underscore the risks of ineffective or counterproductive fairness interventions when not carefully tailored. Our findings highlight the necessity of tailoring bias mitigation strategies to specific datasets and contexts, providing actionable insights for developing equitable, diverse, and inclusive AI systems that are fair and reliable in the criminal justice system.

sample_claims.text: The lending model satisfies demographic parity constraints with quantifiable bounds on both error rate and fairness violation
On held-out data, the shortlisting model's selection rates differ between gender groups by no more than the agreed tolerance.
The recidivism model's true-positive and false-positive rates differ across racial groups by less than the agreed tolerance, and the accuracy cost against the unconstrained model is reported.
Across a sweep of tolerance settings, the model's error and fairness violation trace out a reported trade-off curve, and the deployed setting is justified from it.

techniques.name: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
techniques.description: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations (LAFTR) trains an encoder that turns each record into a representation, a vector of learned features, from which a protected attribute is hard to recover, so that models later built on that representation by other parties, including for prediction tasks not known in advance, also treat groups fairly. It was designed for a data owner who shares encoded data with downstream model builders and cannot control how they train. During training, the encoder, a decoder that reconstructs the input and a classifier for the original task play against an adversary network that tries to predict the protected attribute from the representation; the encoder is updated to defeat the adversary while keeping the information the other two need. The adversary's objective is matched to demographic parity, equalised odds or equal opportunity, and the authors prove that an optimal adversary's objective bounds that unfairness measure for any classifier trained on the representation (for the two error-rate measures the adversary also sees the labels used in training, so the attribute is hidden given the label, and the bound is with respect to those labels). The output is a frozen encoder, delivered with the accuracy and fairness of classifiers trained on top of it.

example_use_cases.description: A data marketplace that supplies customer records to advertisers wants assurance that the targeting models advertisers build will not show offers to men and women at different rates. It trains LAFTR with the demographic parity adversary, releases only the encoded features, and audits a sample of advertisers' models for the gap in positive rates and for how well a fresh classifier can recover gender from the released features.

A health insurer's data team shares encoded claims and prescription data with external analytics suppliers who build their own risk models. It trains LAFTR with an equalised-odds adversary on a comorbidity-risk task, with patients aged 70 or over as the protected group, then measures error-rate gaps for classifiers trained on held-out condition-prediction tasks, because fairness on those new tasks has to be measured rather than assumed.

A hospital imaging research group compares LAFTR with standard training for a chest X-ray triage classifier, with patient sex as the protected attribute and the model-selection rule fixed in advance, to decide whether debiasing the representation narrows the gap in error rates enough to justify its extra training cost.

limitations.description: The fairness bound holds only for an optimal adversary. A weak or under-trained adversary underestimates how much protected information the representation still carries, so downstream models can be less fair than training suggested; the authors report uneven results in places, which they attribute to unstable adversarial training. Audit downstream models directly, including with a fresh classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation.

Transfer to new tasks is not guaranteed for the error-rate criteria. The equalised-odds and equal-opportunity adversaries use the original task's labels, so fairness on a new task with different labels is an empirical result: in the paper's health-data experiment LAFTR was the fairest method on seven of ten transfer tasks, and the authors leave open which tasks transfer fairly.

As formulated, it handles one binary protected attribute and a binary task label; intersectional groups, several attributes or multi-class outcomes need an extension. Training needs the protected attribute and, for the error-rate criteria, the task labels. In the paper's experiments the encoder also took the protected attribute as input, so it is needed whenever new records are encoded; no results are reported without it.

Measured gains can be small in practice. MEDFAIR, a peer-reviewed benchmark of eleven bias-mitigation methods including LAFTR on medical imaging datasets, found the methods did not significantly improve fairness over standard training when trained and tested on the same task, including across datasets (it did not test transfer to new tasks), and that the model-selection criterion changed fairness results substantially. Compare against a standard model under a selection rule stated in advance.

Up to four networks (encoder, decoder, classifier, adversary) are trained against each other, with three weights balancing accuracy, reconstruction and fairness. The paper argues reconstruction is needed for transfer and used different weights for fair classification (accuracy 1, reconstruction 0) and for transfer (accuracy 0, reconstruction 1), so settings do not carry over. The 2018 reference code pins Python 3.6 and TensorFlow 1.9; reimplementations sit inside research benchmarks.

resources.title: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
resources.abstract: In this paper, we advocate for representation learning as the key to mitigating unfair prediction outcomes downstream. Motivated by a scenario where learned representations are used by third parties with unknown objectives, we propose and explore adversarial representation learning as a natural method of ensuring those parties act fairly. We connect group fairness (demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity) to different adversarial objectives. Through worst-case theoretical guarantees and experimental validation, we show that the choice of this objective is crucial to fair prediction. Furthermore, we present the first in-depth experimental demonstration of fair transfer learning and demonstrate empirically that our learned representations admit fair predictions on new tasks while maintaining utility, an essential goal of fair representation learning.

resources.title: MEDFAIR: Benchmarking Fairness for Medical Imaging
resources.abstract: A multitude of work has shown that machine learning-based medical diagnosis systems can be biased against certain subgroups of people. This has motivated a growing number of bias mitigation algorithms that aim to address fairness issues in machine learning. However, it is difficult to compare their effectiveness in medical imaging for two reasons. First, there is little consensus on the criteria to assess fairness. Second, existing bias mitigation algorithms are developed under different settings, e.g., datasets, model selection strategies, backbones, and fairness metrics, making a direct comparison and evaluation based on existing results impossible. In this work, we introduce MEDFAIR, a framework to benchmark the fairness of machine learning models for medical imaging. MEDFAIR covers eleven algorithms from various categories, nine datasets from different imaging modalities, and three model selection criteria. Through extensive experiments, we find that the under-studied issue of model selection criterion can have a significant impact on fairness outcomes; while in contrast, state-of-the-art bias mitigation algorithms do not significantly improve fairness outcomes over empirical risk minimization (ERM) in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. We evaluate fairness from various perspectives and make recommendations for different medical application scenarios that require different ethical principles. Our framework provides a reproducible and easy-to-use entry point for the development and evaluation of future bias mitigation algorithms in deep learning. Code is available at https://github.com/ys-zong/MEDFAIR.

sample_claims.text: Classifiers trained by external parties on the released representation show a demographic parity difference below the agreed threshold on every downstream task audited.

A classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation released under the demographic parity objective does no better than always predicting the majority group, within an agreed margin.
The fairness of downstream risk models built on the shared encoded data was measured on each new prediction task rather than assumed from the task the encoder was trained on.
Under a model-selection rule fixed in advance, the debiased imaging model narrows the gap in error rates between patient groups relative to standard training by a measured margin.

techniques.name: Data Poisoning Detection
techniques.description: Data poisoning detection looks for training examples that an attacker has planted to change how a model behaves. The best-studied case is the backdoor: a few examples carrying a hidden trigger, such as a sticker on a stop sign, are mislabelled so that the model misclassifies any input with the trigger while it performs normally on clean data. Detection first trains a model on the untrusted data, then examines how that model represents each training example internally (its activations in the last hidden layer), one class at a time. Activation clustering splits a class into two groups by those activations and flags the smaller group when the split is clear, and spectral signatures score each example by its position along the main direction of variation and flag the highest scores. The flagged examples are reviewed or removed and the model is retrained, which yields a list of suspected examples and a measure of how cleanly each class separates.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a traffic-sign classifier for a driver-assistance system trains a trial model on images gathered from several suppliers and runs activation clustering on each class. A small separate group of stop-sign images labelled as speed limits, all carrying the same sticker, is flagged and removed before the final training run.

A research platform builds a chest X-ray classifier from images contributed by many partner hospitals. Before any partner's images enter the training set, it trains a trial model and scores each class for the small, separable group of examples a planted backdoor leaves, because one contributor's data could be compromised.

A platform trains a harmful-content classifier on labels supplied by crowd workers. Analysts scan each class for a small separate group of examples sharing a trigger phrase and labelled as harmless, which would let that phrase slip past the filter, and remove them before retraining.

An insurer trains a damage-assessment classifier on claims photos labelled by an outside vendor. Before relying on the labels, it scores each class for a small, separate group of photos carrying the same mark and labelled undamaged, which a compromised vendor account could have planted so that damaged vehicles with the mark pass unchecked. Flagged photos go back to the vendor for explanation.

limitations.description: An attacker who knows the detector can adapt. Both methods rely on poisoned examples standing out in the model's learned representation, so an attack that keeps them close to genuine examples can slip through. Chen et al. found no obvious way round activation clustering within their threat model, but say further work is needed.

False alarms can remove legitimate but unusual examples, reducing data quality and diversity. Chen et al. suggest a silhouette-score cut-off of about 0.10 to 0.15 based on three datasets; another data type or model may need different values, and a wrong value either removes good data or leaves poison in.

Both methods assume poisoned examples are a minority that separates from clean ones in the learned representation, and Tran et al.'s needs an upper bound on how many there are. They were designed and tested on backdoors in image and text classifiers, so attacks that only lower overall accuracy lie outside what the original papers show.

Both methods first train a model on the untrusted data, read its internal activations, then retrain after removing flagged examples. They need the full training data and white-box access to the model, and cost at least two training runs, so they cannot be applied to a model someone else trained when the data or weights are unavailable.

Real poison is unlabelled, so a detector's accuracy can only be measured on poison the tester injects, and a clean result shows that this detector found nothing, not that the data is clean. Telling poison from naturally unusual data is hard.

resources.title: Detecting Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks by Activation Clustering
resources.abstract: While machine learning (ML) models are being increasingly trusted to make decisions in different and varying areas, the safety of systems using such models has become an increasing concern. In particular, ML models are often trained on data from potentially untrustworthy sources, providing adversaries with the opportunity to manipulate them by inserting carefully crafted samples into the training set. Recent work has shown that this type of attack, called a poisoning attack, allows adversaries to insert backdoors or trojans into the model, enabling malicious behavior with simple external backdoor triggers at inference time and only a blackbox perspective of the model itself. Detecting this type of attack is challenging because the unexpected behavior occurs only when a backdoor trigger, which is known only to the adversary, is present. Model users, either direct users of training data or users of pre-trained model from a catalog, may not guarantee the safe operation of their ML-based system. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to backdoor detection and removal for neural networks. Through extensive experimental results, we demonstrate its effectiveness for neural networks classifying text and images. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first methodology capable of detecting poisonous data crafted to insert backdoors and repairing the model that does not require a verified and trusted dataset.

resources.title: Spectral Signatures in Backdoor Attacks
resources.abstract: A recent line of work has uncovered a new form of data poisoning: so-called \emph{backdoor} attacks. These attacks are particularly dangerous because they do not affect a network's behavior on typical, benign data. Rather, the network only deviates from its expected output when triggered by a perturbation planted by an adversary. In this paper, we identify a new property of all known backdoor attacks, which we call \emph{spectral signatures}. This property allows us to utilize tools from robust statistics to thwart the attacks. We demonstrate the efficacy of these signatures in detecting and removing poisoned examples on real image sets and state of the art neural network architectures. We believe that understanding spectral signatures is a crucial first step towards designing ML systems secure against such backdoor attacks

resources.title: SAFELOC: Overcoming Data Poisoning Attacks in Heterogeneous Federated Machine Learning for Indoor Localization
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) based indoor localization solutions are critical for many emerging applications, yet their efficacy is often compromised by hardware/software variations across mobile devices (i.e., device heterogeneity) and the threat of ML data poisoning attacks. Conventional methods aimed at countering these challenges show limited resilience to the uncertainties created by these phenomena. In response, in this paper, we introduce SAFELOC, a novel framework that not only minimizes localization errors under these challenging conditions but also ensures model compactness for efficient mobile device deployment. Our framework targets a distributed and co-operative learning environment that uses federated learning (FL) to preserve user data privacy and assumes heterogeneous mobile devices carried by users (just like in most real-world scenarios). Within this heterogeneous FL context, SAFELOC introduces a novel fused neural network architecture that performs data poisoning detection and localization, with a low model footprint. Additionally, a dynamic saliency map-based aggregation strategy is designed to adapt based on the severity of the detected data poisoning scenario. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that SAFELOC achieves improvements of up to 5.9x in mean localization error, 7.8x in worst-case localization error, and a 2.1x reduction in model inference latency compared to state-of-the-art indoor localization frameworks, across diverse building floorplans, mobile devices, and ML data poisoning attack scenarios.

resources.title: Zero-Shot Detection and Sanitization of Data Poisoning Attacks in Wearable AI Using Large Language Models
resources.abstract: Wearable AI systems, particularly in Human Activity Recognition (HAR), are becoming integral to applications in healthcare, security, and personal fitness due to the widespread adoption of smart devices and wearable technologies. However, the increasing reliance on machine learning models in HAR introduces significant risks, especially from poisoning attacks that compromise system reliability and data integrity. This paper explores the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) to detect and sanitize poisoning attacks in wearable AI systems. Building on ongoing research into integrating LLMs within cyber-physical systems, we focus on sensor-based interactions with the physical world. Our case study seeks to answer the following question: How effective are LLMs in detecting and sanitizing poisoning attacks on human activity sensor data? Through zero-shot learning, we evaluate the performance of models such as ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4, and Gemini, providing insights into the viability of LLMs for real-time defense and data integrity in wearable AI systems.

techniques.name: AutoAttack
techniques.description: AutoAttack is a fixed suite of four automated adversarial attacks, introduced by Croce and Hein (ICML 2020), that measures how much of an image classifier's test accuracy survives small, deliberately chosen changes to its input images at inference time. The evaluator states the threat model, a norm and radius that bound the change (for example, no pixel value changed by more than 8/255 under the L-infinity norm), and the standard version then attacks each correctly classified test image in turn with APGD-CE (projected gradient descent that sets its own step size, on the cross-entropy loss), a targeted APGD on the authors' Difference of Logits Ratio loss, a targeted form of the FAB minimum-norm attack, and the Square Attack, which needs only the model's outputs and so still works when gradients are uninformative. An image counts as robust only if none of the four finds a misclassified version within the bound, and because every attack setting is fixed in advance the evaluator tunes nothing, which removes a common cause of overstated robustness: an attack too weakly tuned for the model. The output is robust accuracy, the share of test images still classified correctly under attack at the stated norm and radius, reported beside clean accuracy; published models are compared on the RobustBench leaderboard, which uses AutoAttack as its standard evaluation. Because AutoAttack is not built around any one defence, it can supply the attack step for a wider judgement of a defence, such as whether adversarial training holds up against attacks it was not trained on; unlike red teaming, it involves no human attacker or open-ended search.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model-risk team validating a vendor's classifier that recognises which of 40 identity-document types a customer has photographed during remote account opening, so the right authenticity checks run, receives the model weights under the review agreement. It reruns the vendor's robustness evaluation with standard AutoAttack at the same L-infinity radius, compares the two robust accuracies and records any automatic warnings before accepting the vendor's figure.

A photo-sharing platform's trust-and-safety team expects uploaders to perturb images to slip past the classifier that sorts uploads into a dozen prohibited-content categories and an allowed class. Choosing between two candidate models, it runs standard AutoAttack on both at a perturbation budget agreed with its security team, and selects the one with higher robust accuracy whose clean-accuracy cost is acceptable, recording both figures in the release review.

A research group proposing a new defence for a traffic-sign classifier runs standard AutoAttack before publication and finds that the Square Attack lowers robust accuracy further than the gradient-based attacks, one of AutoAttack's warning signs that gradients are masked. It treats its figure as an upper bound and has an attack designed for its defence built before claiming any robustness.

A computational-pathology group comparing a convolutional network and a vision transformer for three-way tumour subtyping on routine slide images attacks both with AutoAttack, its settings reduced for three classes, at several perturbation sizes below what a blinded clinical reader could detect, and compares attack success rates on an external patient cohort to decide which architecture goes forward.

limitations.description: Robust accuracy from AutoAttack is an upper bound: an image counts as robust because these four attacks failed, not because no adversarial example exists. The authors present it as the minimum test for a new defence rather than the strongest possible attack, so a claim that no change within the bound can alter a decision needs a certified-robustness method instead.

The standard version can overstate robustness for defences that are randomised, not differentiable or run an optimisation loop at inference. The reference code warns about some of these cases, offers a version averaging gradients over the model's randomness, and recommends attacks built for the specific defence; RobustBench excludes such defences. A defence tuned to beat AutoAttack itself can pass it without being robust.

The result holds only for the norm and radius tested. It gives no direct evidence about patches, rotations, physical changes to objects or natural corruptions: in RobustBench's quick-start guide, L-infinity-robust models do much worse than an undefended model on fog-corrupted images, though better on average across corruption types. Benchmark radii such as 8/255 are conventions, so the radius should be justified from the deployment's threat, and a new norm or radius needs a new run.

It needs white-box access: three of the four attacks use the model's gradients, and the code expects raw scores (logits) and inputs scaled to [0, 1]; with access only to output scores, the Square Attack can run alone, a weaker test. The standard settings also assume ten or more classes, since the targeted attacks each try nine other classes; on a binary or few-class model the reference code stops with an error, so the settings must be reduced and the result is no longer the standard one.

The full evaluation is computationally heavy for large models and test sets: each white-box run uses 100 iterations, the targeted attacks each try nine target classes, and the Square Attack makes up to 5,000 queries per image. RobustBench's quick start runs a cheaper two-attack version on 50 images and notes the full version is slower but more accurate; a figure from a subset should be reported with its sampling error.

resources.title: Reliable evaluation of adversarial robustness with an ensemble of diverse parameter-free attacks
resources.abstract: The field of defense strategies against adversarial attacks has significantly grown over the last years, but progress is hampered as the evaluation of adversarial defenses is often insufficient and thus gives a wrong impression of robustness. Many promising defenses could be broken later on, making it difficult to identify the state-of-the-art. Frequent pitfalls in the evaluation are improper tuning of hyperparameters of the attacks, gradient obfuscation or masking. In this paper we first propose two extensions of the PGD-attack overcoming failures due to suboptimal step size and problems of the objective function. We then combine our novel attacks with two complementary existing ones to form a parameter-free, computationally affordable and user-independent ensemble of attacks to test adversarial robustness. We apply our ensemble to over 50 models from papers published at recent top machine learning and computer vision venues. In all except one of the cases we achieve lower robust test accuracy than reported in these papers, often by more than $10\%$, identifying several broken defenses.

techniques.name: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
techniques.description: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) trains a neural network, or another model fitted by gradient descent, so that the finished model carries a formal differential privacy guarantee about the individual examples it was trained on. Differential privacy is more often applied by adding calibrated noise to the answer of a query or to a published statistic; DP-SGD instead changes the training algorithm itself. At each step it draws a random batch, computes the gradient (the direction in which an example pushes the model's parameters) separately for every example, scales down any gradient longer than a fixed clipping bound, adds Gaussian noise proportional to that bound to the sum, and updates the model with the noisy average, so that no single example can move the model by much and what influence remains is masked. A privacy accountant adds up the privacy cost of every step from the noise level, the sampling rate and the number of steps, and reports the total as epsilon and delta: epsilon limits how much more likely any trained model is with a given example in the training data than without it, and delta is a small probability that this limit fails. The output is a trained model with a stated (epsilon, delta) guarantee, which also covers anything later computed from the model, including its predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank wants to give a credit-default model to a partner lender, which will hold the model weights. Its data science team trains the model with DP-SGD in Opacus, with each customer contributing one training example so that the guarantee protects a customer, targets epsilon 2 at a delta below one over the number of customers, and records the noise multiplier, clipping bound, sampling rate and accountant output in the model's release file.

A consortium of hospitals publishes the weights of a chest X-ray classifier so that other hospitals can fine-tune it locally. It trains with DP-SGD using one image per patient, replaces the network's batch normalisation layers with group normalisation as Opacus requires, and publishes the (epsilon, delta) guarantee and its unit, one patient, with the weights so that receiving hospitals can cite it in their own assessments.

A recruitment platform fine-tunes a language model, pretrained on public text, on job applicants' CVs (one per applicant) to suggest skills tags. It fine-tunes with DP-SGD, adds the cost of the hyperparameter search it ran on the CVs to the privacy budget, and compares tagging accuracy with a non-private fine-tune to decide whether the accuracy cost at its chosen epsilon is acceptable.

limitations.description: Clipping and noise reduce accuracy, and the reduction is not shared evenly: classes and groups that are rare in the training data lose the most, so a private model can widen an existing accuracy gap between groups. In the original experiments the drop at epsilon 8 was about 1 percentage point on handwritten digits but about 7 on a harder ten-class image task. Accuracy should be reported per group, and pretraining on public data or more training data is often needed to keep the cost acceptable.

The stated epsilon holds only if the code matches the accountant's assumptions. The usual accountants assume each batch is drawn by including every example independently at random, but many pipelines shuffle the data and cut it into fixed batches; an audit of models trained that way measured privacy loss up to four times the epsilon they reported. A claim should name the sampling method and accountant, and differential privacy auditing can test the figure empirically.

The guarantee protects one training example, not one person. If a patient has ten admissions or a customer hundreds of messages in the training set, their protection is much weaker than epsilon suggests, because the bound loosens with the number of examples they contribute. Capping each person's contribution, or making each person a single example, gives a guarantee at the level of the person, at some cost in data and accuracy.

No agreed value of epsilon makes a model private, and large values are common: the method's original headline results used epsilon 8, at which a training outcome may be about 3,000 times more likely with a given example than without it, and the Opacus image tutorial targets 50. Hyperparameter searches run on the private data also leak information unless their cost is added to the budget. A claim should state epsilon, delta, the unit of privacy and what the budget covers.

Computing a separate gradient for every example costs memory and time; in the original experiments one training epoch went from about 40 to about 180 seconds. Layers that combine examples within a batch, such as batch normalisation, break the per-example bound and must be replaced, for example with group normalisation, so an existing architecture may need changing and re-tuning before it can be trained privately.

resources.title: Private Ad Modeling with DP-SGD
resources.abstract: A well-known algorithm in privacy-preserving ML is differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). While this algorithm has been evaluated on text and image data, it has not been previously applied to ads data, which are notorious for their high class imbalance and sparse gradient updates. In this work we apply DP-SGD to several ad modeling tasks including predicting click-through rates, conversion rates, and number of conversion events, and evaluate their privacy-utility trade-off on real-world datasets. Our work is the first to empirically demonstrate that DP-SGD can provide both privacy and utility for ad modeling tasks.

The published chest X-ray model weights satisfy differential privacy with epsilon 8 and delta 10^-5 with respect to any one patient, and the hyperparameter search run on patient images is included in that budget.
Training batches were drawn by Poisson sampling, matching the assumption of the privacy accountant that produced the reported epsilon.
The skills-tagging model's privacy budget of epsilon 4 per applicant covers the full fine-tuning run and every hyperparameter trial run on applicants' CVs.

techniques.name: GNNExplainer
techniques.description: GNNExplainer explains one prediction of a graph neural network, a model that passes information along the edges of a graph such as a molecule, a payment network or a mesh of weather grid points, by finding a small subgraph and a small set of input features that most support that prediction. Explanation methods for flat inputs, such as SHAP and LIME, give each input feature its own score and have no built-in notion of a connection between two nodes; this method scores the connections themselves, restricted to the part of the graph the model actually reads for the prediction (its computation graph, the neighbourhood within as many hops as the model has message-passing layers). It learns a mask with a value between 0 and 1 for each edge of that computation graph and for each node-feature dimension by gradient descent: the masked graph is fed to the model, and the masks are adjusted to keep the predicted label as likely as possible while penalties keep the total mask small and push values towards 0 or 1. Edges and features whose mask values fall below a threshold are then dropped, leaving a compact subgraph and feature subset that can be drawn over the input graph; the same procedure explains node labels, predicted links and whole-graph labels, and the original paper also aligns the explanations of many nodes of one class into a summary pattern. It needs gradient access to the model, and each explanation is a separate optimisation.

example_use_cases.description: A pharmaceutical company's computational toxicology team uses a graph neural network to flag candidate molecules as likely mutagenic. For each flagged compound it reviews the substructure and atom features GNNExplainer selects and checks them against known structural alerts such as nitro groups, to decide whether a flag rests on chemistry the team recognises before the compound is deprioritised.

A bank's financial-crime unit scores accounts with a graph neural network over its payment network to flag likely money-mule accounts. Investigators receive with each flag the explanation subgraph of counterparties and transfers and the account features it selected, and use them to decide whether to escalate; model validators sample explanations to check that flags do not rest mainly on features such as branch or account-opening channel.

A weather service's model evaluation team runs the regression mode of the PyTorch Geometric implementation on a small set of high-impact forecasts from a graph-based forecasting model, such as the predicted rainfall total at one location. Forecasters check whether the connections and input variables selected, for example humidity upwind, are physically plausible, and the team deletes the selected connections to confirm the forecast changes, before such forecasts feed a warning service.

limitations.description: Each explanation is a separate optimisation, run for a set number of steps (100 by default in the PyTorch Geometric implementation), so explaining many nodes or graphs is slow and explanations of similar cases are not required to agree. A view of the model as a whole needs an extra step, such as the class-level summary in the original paper, or a method that trains one explainer for all instances.

The masks are soft during optimisation, so the model is run on graphs whose edges and features are scaled by fractions it never saw in training, and these values can add meaning or noise of their own. The objective is not convex and the masks start at random: in a 2024 benchmark, the ten-edge explanations from runs with different seeds overlapped by a Jaccard index of only 0.18 to 0.80 across six datasets. The final subgraph also depends on the threshold used to cut the mask.

The size of the explanation is set by the user, not found. The original experiments fixed it at the known size of the planted pattern on synthetic graphs and at 10 edges and 5 features on real ones, and the PyTorch Geometric implementation advises tuning the size penalty to the graph's average degree. A compact explanation can therefore leave out structure the model uses.

Most evidence that it finds the right structure comes from synthetic graphs with planted patterns, and a trained model need not use the planted edges, so agreement with them can mislead. A 2023 benchmark found graph explainers, this one included, less faithful when linked nodes tend to differ and when the deciding structure is large. Check fidelity on your own model, for example by deleting the explanation and measuring the change.

It assumes the computation graph is small. The computation graph grows with every message-passing layer, so in a mesh-based forecasting model that passes messages many times along long-range edges (GraphCast uses 16 such layers) it probably spans most of the mesh: the mask then covers most edges and compactness comes from the size penalty, not the model. This has not been tested. PyTorch Geometric applies the mask inside its own message-passing layers, so the model must use them or be adapted.

resources.title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
resources.abstract:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a powerful tool for machine learning on graphs.GNNs combine node feature information with the graph structure by 
recursively passing neural messages along edges of the input graph. However, incorporating both graph structure and feature information leads to complex models,
and explaining predictions made by GNNs remains unsolved. Here
we propose GNNExplainer, the first general, model-agnostic approach for providing interpretable explanations for predictions of any GNN-based model on any graph-based machine learning task. Given an instance, GNNExplainer identifies a compact subgraph structure and a small subset of node features that have a crucial role in GNN's prediction. 
Further, GNNExplainer  can generate consistent and concise explanations for an entire class of instances.
We formulate GNNExplainer as an optimization task that maximizes the mutual information between a GNN's prediction and distribution of possible subgraph structures. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs show that our approach can identify important graph structures as well as node features, and outperforms baselines by 17.1% on average. GNNExplainer  provides a variety of benefits, from the ability to visualize semantically relevant structures to interpretability, to giving insights into errors of faulty GNNs.
